title: Case Study: LRU Cache
summary: Design a cache that evicts the least-recently-used item — and do every operation in O(1). One HashMap, one doubly linked list.

blocks.markdown:
An **LRU (Least Recently Used) cache** holds a fixed number of items. When it's full and a new item arrives, it evicts the item that was **used longest ago**.

- Fixed **capacity**, set at construction.
- `get(key)` — return the value, or miss; also counts as a "use."
- `put(key, value)` — insert or update; evicts the LRU item on overflow.
- The interview bar: every operation must run in **O(1)**, not O(n).

blocks.subTitle: Why it's a classic LLD question
blocks.markdown:
It looks like a two-method class, but it forces you to combine two data structures correctly under a hard constraint.

- A **HashMap alone** gives O(1) lookup but no sense of "order of use."
- A **linked list alone** gives ordering but O(n) lookup.
- Neither works solo. The design insight — pairing them — is exactly what interviewers probe.

The standard solution: a **HashMap** mapping `key → node`, plus a **doubly linked list (DLL)** holding those same nodes in recency order, most-recently-used at the **head**, least-recently-used at the **tail**.

- HashMap gives O(1) **access** to any node by key.
- DLL gives O(1) **reordering** — move a node to the front, or drop the tail — without shifting anything else.
- Together: O(1) lookup **and** O(1) recency tracking.

blocks.subTitle: Why not just a plain array or singly linked list
blocks.markdown:
An **array** needs shifting elements to reorder or evict — O(n). A **singly linked list** lets you move forward but not detach a node in O(1), because removing a node needs its **predecessor**, which a singly linked list can't reach without a scan.

- A **doubly linked list** stores both `prev` and `next` on every node.
- That lets you unlink any node — front, middle, or tail — in true O(1), no traversal.

How the two structures line up:

Every HashMap entry points straight at its node — no searching the list to find it.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: the Node
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Node:
    key
    value
    prev    // pointer to previous node (towards head)
    next    // pointer to next node (towards tail)

    constructor(key, value):
        this.key = key
        this.value = value
        this.prev = null
        this.next = null
```

Storing `key` on the node matters: when the tail is evicted, you need its key to delete it from the HashMap too.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: DLL helpers
blocks.markdown:
```text
// head and tail are dummy sentinel nodes — they never hold real data.
// This means every real node always has a non-null prev and next,
// so no special-casing for "empty list" or "first/last real node."

method addFront(node):
    node.prev = head
    node.next = head.next
    head.next.prev = node
    head.next = node

method remove(node):
    node.prev.next = node.next
    node.next.prev = node.prev

method moveToFront(node):
    remove(node)
    addFront(node)

method removeLast():
    lru = tail.prev
    remove(lru)
    return lru
```

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: LRUCache.get()
blocks.markdown:
```text
class LRUCache:
    capacity
    map          // key -> Node
    head, tail   // dummy sentinels, head.next ... tail.prev holds real nodes

    constructor(capacity):
        this.capacity = capacity
        this.map = new HashMap()
        this.head = new Node(null, null)
        this.tail = new Node(null, null)
        head.next = tail
        tail.prev = head

    method get(key):
        if key not in map:
            return MISS
        node = map[key]
        moveToFront(node)   // touching it makes it most-recently-used
        return node.value
```

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: LRUCache.put()
blocks.markdown:
```text
    method put(key, value):
        if key in map:
            node = map[key]
            node.value = value
            moveToFront(node)
            return

        if map.size == capacity:
            lru = removeLast()      // evict tail — least recently used
            map.delete(lru.key)

        newNode = new Node(key, value)
        map[key] = newNode
        addFront(newNode)
```

blocks.subTitle: Why sentinels
blocks.markdown:
The dummy `head` and `tail` nodes hold no data — they're **sentinels** that simplify every list operation.

- Without them, adding to an empty list or removing the only node needs special-case branches.
- With them, `head.next` is always "most recent real node" and `tail.prev` is always "least recent real node," even when the cache is empty or has one item.
- Fewer edge cases means fewer bugs in an interview setting.

**Time:** `get` and `put` are both **O(1)**. HashMap lookup is O(1); every DLL operation (`addFront`, `remove`, `moveToFront`, `removeLast`) touches a fixed number of pointers, never scanning the list.

**Space:** **O(capacity)** — one node plus one HashMap entry per cached item, regardless of how many `get`/`put` calls happen over time.

blocks.subTitle: Thread safety
blocks.markdown:
A plain LRU cache isn't safe under concurrent access — two threads calling `put` at once can corrupt the DLL's pointers.

- Simplest fix: wrap `get`/`put` in a single **mutex/lock** — correct, but serializes all access.
- Better throughput: a **read-write lock**, or shard the cache into N independent LRU caches by key hash to cut lock contention.
- See [concurrency-in-oo-design](concurrency-in-oo-design) for the underlying locking patterns.

blocks.subTitle: TTL (time-to-live)
blocks.markdown:
Real caches (Redis, browser caches) often expire entries after a fixed time, independent of recency.

- Add an `expiresAt` timestamp to each `Node`.
- `get` checks the timestamp first — if expired, treat it as a miss and evict immediately.
- A background sweep can also walk expired entries, but the **lazy check on read** is what keeps `get` O(1).

Two eviction strategies, different signals.

| Aspect | LRU | LFU |
|---|---|---|
| Evicts by | Longest since last use | Fewest total uses |
| Structure | HashMap + DLL | HashMap + frequency buckets |

LRU is simpler and handles shifting access patterns well; LFU protects "steady favorites" from a burst of one-off reads, at the cost of extra bookkeeping.

Common mistakes in this design:

- **Using a singly linked list.** You can't remove an arbitrary node in O(1) without its `prev` pointer.
- **Forgetting to move a node on `get`.** A read is a use — skip the `moveToFront` and eviction order becomes wrong.
- **Not storing the key on the Node.** Without it, evicting the tail leaves a dangling, undeletable entry in the HashMap.

blocks.subTitle: Why HashMap + DLL
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why does an LRU cache need both a HashMap and a doubly linked list?**

Each alone can't hit O(1) on both operations. A HashMap gives O(1) key lookup but no cheap way to track usage order. A linked list gives cheap reordering but O(n) lookup by key. Combining them — map to node, list for order — gets O(1) on `get` and `put` together.

blocks.subTitle: Why doubly, not singly, linked
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why a doubly linked list instead of a singly linked one?**

Removing a node from the middle of a list requires updating its predecessor's `next` pointer. A singly linked list can't find that predecessor without scanning from the head — O(n). Storing `prev` on every node makes removal, and therefore eviction and move-to-front, true O(1).

blocks.subTitle: Making it thread-safe
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How would you make this LRU cache thread-safe?**

Wrap `get` and `put` in a lock, since both read and mutate the shared map and list. A single mutex is simplest but serializes everything; for higher throughput, shard the cache by key hash into several independent LRU instances, each with its own lock, cutting contention.

blocks.subTitle: LRU vs LFU
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When would you pick LFU over LRU?**

When access frequency matters more than recency — e.g. a cache where a few items are hit constantly but occasionally interrupted by a burst of unrelated one-time reads. LRU would wrongly evict the steady favorites; LFU's frequency count protects them, at the cost of tracking counts per key.

blocks.subTitle: What happens on capacity overflow
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Walk through what happens when `put` is called on a full cache.**

The key isn't already in the map, and `map.size == capacity`, so the cache evicts first: `removeLast()` unlinks the tail's neighbor (the true LRU node) and returns it, then its key is deleted from the map. Only then is the new node created, inserted into the map, and added to the front of the list.
